Fit a ctsem model

Source: R/ctFit.R
ctFit.Rd

Fits a ctsem model specified via ctModel with type either 'ct' or 'dt'. ctStanFit is maintained as a backward-compatible alias.

Usage

ctFit(
  datalong,
  model,
  stanmodeltext = NA,
  iter = 1000,
  intoverstates = TRUE,
  binomial = FALSE,
  fit = TRUE,
  intoverpop = "auto",
  poprank = "auto",
  sameInitialTimes = FALSE,
  stationary = FALSE,
  plot = FALSE,
  derrind = NA,
  optimize = TRUE,
  optimcontrol = list(),
  backend = c("julia", "stan"),
  nlcontrol = list(),
  nopriors = NA,
  priors = FALSE,
  chains = 2,
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 2L),
  inits = NULL,
  compileArgs = list(),
  forcerecompile = FALSE,
  saveCompile = TRUE,
  savescores = FALSE,
  savesubjectmatrices = FALSE,
  saveComplexPars = FALSE,
  gendata = FALSE,
  sampleControl = list(),
  control = list(),
  verbose = 0,
  ...,
  popunique = NULL,
  popblocks = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  ctstanmodel
)

Arguments

datalong

long format data containing columns for subject id, time, manifest variables, any time dependent (i.e. varying within subject) predictors, and any time independent (not varying within subject) predictors.

model

model object as generated by ctModel with type='ct' or 'dt', for continuous or discrete time models respectively.

stanmodeltext

already specified Stan model character string, generally leave NA unless modifying Stan model directly. (Possible after modification of output from fitting with argument fit=FALSE.) backend='stan' only.

iter

Deprecated, use sampleControl$iter. Still honoured, with a warning.

intoverstates

Logical. TRUE (the default) integrates over the latent states with a Kalman filter. FALSE estimates the states along with the parameters, and the fit reports their trajectory in fit$estimate$states. FALSE is for sampling (optimize=FALSE). With backend='julia' it avoids the Gaussian approximation the filter makes for binary, ordinal and count indicators. optimize=TRUE is refused, because the joint mode of states and parameters is not a useful estimate. With optimcontrol$estonly=TRUE the mode is returned anyway, without standard errors.

binomial

Deprecated. Logical indicating the use of binary rather than Gaussian data, as with IRT analyses. This now sets the manifesttype of every indicator to 1, for binary.

fit

If FALSE, the model and data are prepared but not fitted. With backend='stan' the unfitted fit object is returned, and with backend='julia' the specification passed to the engine.

intoverpop

How random effects (individual differences) are handled: integrated out of the likelihood, or sampled with the other parameters.

'auto', the default, integrates them out when optimizing, as TRUE does, and samples them ('none') when optimize=FALSE. The exception is a julia fit in which every subject's likelihood is Gaussian in its random effects (a linear model with Gaussian indicators, and random effects only on means, with linear transforms). There the random effects are integrated exactly and the population parameters sampled ('laplace').

TRUE integrates them out, by 'laplace' on backend='julia' and by 'augmented' on backend='stan' or with intoverstates=FALSE. fit$args$resolved$intoverpopreason records which was used and why.

'laplace' (backend='julia') integrates random effects on a manifest mean, initial mean or continuous intercept of a linear Gaussian model exactly, and all other random effects by a Laplace approximation.

'augmented' adds each random effect to the states of the Kalman filter. This is exact for random effects on means in a linear Gaussian model, and a linear approximation elsewhere, which shrinks random effects on the dynamics. In a model whose dynamics depend on the state, a random effect on the dynamics or the initial mean can also overstate the likelihood and move the estimates, and variation in DIFFUSION or MANIFESTVAR parameters is only partly identified. ctFit warns in both cases.

'quadrature' (backend='julia', optimizing) fits by 'laplace', then refines the fit by integrating numerically the random effects of the subjects (or groups) that the random-effects check flags (optimcontrol$checks). The reported estimates, standard errors and log likelihood are from the refined fit, with the Laplace log likelihood kept in loglik_laplace. The refinement takes seconds to minutes, longer with nested levels. ctFitUncertainty(fit, intoverpop = 'quadrature') does the same after a fit.

FALSE, or 'none', samples the random effects with the other parameters and needs optimize=FALSE, because maximising over every subject's random effects would drive the population variance to zero. With optimize=FALSE on julia, 'none' samples the joint posterior of parameters and random effects, while 'laplace' and 'augmented' sample the population parameters with the random effects integrated out.

poprank

Rank of the population covariance of the individually varying parameters. NA leaves the covariance unrestricted. A whole number below the number of varying parameters gives a reduced-rank covariance, with fewer parameters and a faster fit, but as an approximation to the full covariance. 'auto', the default, uses the number of varying parameters that affect the expected observations. Under intoverpop='augmented' that is all the data can identify, so the default loses nothing, and a message says when it reduces the rank. Under 'laplace' and 'none' the default leaves the covariance unrestricted, and a rank has to be given explicitly. Requires backend='julia'.

Under 'laplace' and 'none' a rank may be given per grouping level by name, as poprank=c(study=2), and it may not be lower than the number of individually varying T0MEANS with a free T0VAR. Under 'augmented' a model with a varying T0MEANS keeps full rank, and an explicit rank is refused. A reduced covariance is L %*% t(L) for a loading matrix L, reported as poploading_<parameter>_dim<j>.<level>. The sign of a loading is arbitrary, so interpret the standard deviations and correlations that summary() reports. A stated RAWPOPVAR cell switches the default reduction off, and cannot be combined with an explicit rank. The rank may also be set on the model, as model$poprank <- 2. A rank of 0 is allowed at a level where every varying parameter has its own variance (popunique).

sameInitialTimes

if TRUE, include an empty observation for every subject that has no observation at the earliest observation time of the dataset. This ensures that the T0MEANS occurs for every subject at the same time, rather than just at the earliest observation for that subject. Important when modelling trends over time, age, etc.

stationary

Logical. If TRUE, each subject's latent processes start from their stationary distribution, with the long run mean -DRIFT^-1 CINT and the asymptotic covariance, and T0MEANS and T0VAR are not estimated. This suits processes observed long after they began. Requires backend='julia', a continuous time model, and DRIFT, CINT and DIFFUSION matrices that do not depend on the latent states or on time dependent predictors. Individual differences in those matrices are allowed with intoverpop='laplace', which intoverpop='auto' then chooses, and each subject then starts from its own stationary distribution. A latent process whose DRIFT is fixed so that it never settles, such as a row fixed at zero or the clock of ctModelPeriodicComponent, is refused.

To start only some initial conditions at stationarity, name those cells 'stationary' in the model (backend='julia'). Other initial conditions stay as written. A T0MEANS cell takes its entry of the stationary mean (asymCINT). A T0VAR diagonal cell gives its latent the stationary variance (the diagonal of asymDIFFUSION) and keeps its T0VAR correlations with the other latents. A T0VAR off-diagonal cell gives the pair the stationary covariance, and needs both their variances, and every covariance among the latents it joins, named too. The stationary distribution is computed for the marked latents and the latents that drive them, so DRIFT, CINT and DIFFUSION need to be fixed within each subject only for those latents.

plot

if TRUE, for sampling, a Shiny program is launched upon fitting to interactively plot samples. May struggle with many (e.g., > 5000) parameters. For optimizing, the optimisation trace is plotted, with backend='julia' after the fit returns. For live output during a julia fit use optimcontrol$callback.

derrind

deprecated, latents involved in dynamic error calculations are determined automatically now.

optimize

if TRUE, estimate by optimisation (maximum likelihood, or maximum a posteriori with priors=TRUE), with standard errors from the curvature at the estimate. If FALSE, sample the posterior, with Stan's HMC sampler for backend='stan' and with NUTS or tempered SMC for backend='julia' (see sampleControl). Sampling is slower, but does not rely on a normal approximation at the estimate. Other uncertainty methods for an optimised fit, including importance sampling, are in ctFitUncertainty. The point estimate of a sampled fit is the median of the draws for each parameter on stan (fit$stanfit$rawest), and their mean on julia (fit$estimate$raw).

optimcontrol

List of optimiser settings, with the same meaning on both backends: stopping rules (tol, g_tol, maxiter), starting values (initsd, carefulfit), the uncertainty computed at the end (uncertainty, estonly), and optional stages such as stochastic, and saem and checks under intoverpop='laplace'. ctOptimControl lists every setting with its backend and default. A misspelled name, or one the backend does not support, is an error.

backend

Either 'julia' (the default) or 'stan'. Both take the same model specification and give the same summaries. Only the julia backend has intoverpop='laplace', grouping levels above the subject, and ordinal, count and censored indicators, and it handles binary indicators more accurately. It needs Julia, which ctJuliaInstall sets up (see also ctJuliaSetup). The stan backend needs no other software, and will be deprecated.

nlcontrol

List of non-linear control parameters. maxtimestep must be a positive numeric, specifying the largest time span covered by the numerical integration. The large default ensures that for each observation time interval, only a single step of exponential integration is used. When maxtimestep is smaller than the observation time interval, the integration is nested within an Euler like loop. Smaller values may offer greater accuracy, but are slower and not always necessary. Given the exponential integration, linear model elements are fit exactly with only a single step. With backend='julia', nsubsteps = 'auto' instead measures how nonlinear each observation interval is, at the starting values and again at the optimum, and adds integration steps only to the intervals that need them. substeptol (default 0.01) is the largest acceptable linearisation error, as a fraction of the predicted state standard deviation, and maxsubsteps (default 64) is the most steps for one interval. maxtimestep still limits the step size. The steps chosen are reported in fit$substeps. When sampling, they are chosen at the optimised fit that starts the sampler, and kept for the chains. transition = 'euler' (julia backend with intoverstates = FALSE only) uses Euler-Maruyama steps between substeps instead of the exponential step. This gives a reference free of the filter's approximations, and needs a small maxtimestep. See also ctParticleLik.

nopriors

deprecated, use priors argument. logical. If TRUE, any priors are disabled – sometimes desirable for optimization.

priors

FALSE (the default), TRUE or 'randomCorr'. FALSE uses no priors, giving maximum likelihood estimates. TRUE adds ctsem's normal(0,1) prior on the raw scale to every parameter, giving maximum a posteriori estimates when optimising. 'randomCorr' puts that prior on the random-effect correlations only, at every level, which helps when the data do not determine those correlations well. Sampling (optimize=FALSE) without priors on every parameter gives a warning, because a parameter the data do not determine then has an improper posterior, so use priors=TRUE when sampling. 'randomCorr' needs backend='julia'.

chains

Deprecated, use sampleControl$chains. Still honoured, with a warning.

cores

number of CPU cores to use, either a positive whole number or 'maxneeded' for all but one (at most the number of chains on stan). Defaults to getOption("mc.cores", 2). This is the most cores the call uses at once, including any worker processes it starts. Julia fits with cores > 1 can differ in the last decimal places from run to run, so use cores = 1 when comparing results exactly. The Julia session starts with as many threads as the first call that needs it asks for. A later call asking for more runs with what the session has, and says so. ctJuliaSetup(threads = n, force = TRUE) restarts the session with more threads, and options(ctsem.julia.restart = TRUE) lets a fit restart it when needed.

inits

NULL (the default) for ctsem's own starting values, or a vector of starting values on the raw (unconstrained) scale, one per free parameter, such as fit$estimate$raw from a julia fit or fit$stanfit$rawest from a stan fit. With backend='julia' it may also be a fit, whose estimates are matched to this model's parameters by name, so that a model extended by a predictor or a smooth starts from the earlier estimates with the new coefficients at zero. With backend='stan' and optimize=FALSE, 'optimize' optimises first and starts the chains there.

compileArgs

List of arguments to pass to stan_model for compilation of the Stan model.

forcerecompile

logical. For backend='stan', recompiles the stan model regardless of apparent need (for development). For backend='julia', compiles the model's state-dependent matrix cells and any custom parameter transforms into code for this model, instead of interpreting them. The first fit of the model in a session then takes a minute or more longer, and later computations run up to a third faster for heavily nonlinear models. Only worth it when such a model takes many minutes to fit.

saveCompile

if TRUE and compilation is needed / requested, writes the stan model to the parent frame as ctsem.compiled (unless that object already exists and is not from ctsem), to avoid unnecessary recompilation.

savescores

Logical. If TRUE, output from the Kalman filter is saved in output. For datasets with many variables or time points, will increase file size substantially. backend='stan' only. For julia fits, ctKalman computes it from the fit.

savesubjectmatrices

Logical. If TRUE, subject specific matrices are saved – only relevant when either time dependent predictors or individual differences are used. Can increase memory usage dramatically in large models, and can be computed after fitting using ctExtract or ctSubjectPars. backend='stan' only.

saveComplexPars

Logical. If TRUE, also save rowwise output of any complex parameters specified, i.e. combinations of parameters, functions and states.

gendata

Logical – If TRUE, uses provided data for only covariates and a time and missingness structure, and generates random data according to the specified model / priors. Generated data is in the $Ygen subobject after running extract on the fit object. For datasets with many manifest variables or time points, file size may be large. To generate data based on the posterior of a fitted model, see ctGenerateFromFit. backend='stan' only. For julia, use ctGenerate.

sampleControl

Used when optimize=FALSE: a list of sampler settings. chains is the number of chains (4 on julia, 2 on stan). iter is the number of iterations including warmup (1000). warmup is the number of warmup iterations (200, or half of iter if that is less), and is not used by the map sampler, which has its own warmup. draws is the number of draws after warmup, and overrides iter when given. seed sets the random seed. saveEffects keeps every random-effect draw. processes (FALSE) runs the chains in separate worker processes, at most cores at once, instead of together in this session.

For backend='julia' the list also takes sampler: 'map' (NUTS through a learnt map, the default for the joint posterior), 'saem' or 'nuts'. placement sets where the chains start. The map sampler starts from an optimised fit. For 'saem' and 'nuts' on the joint posterior, the default 'saem' starts them from an SAEM run, with no optimisation needed, and 'fit' starts them around an optimised fit. Sampling stops when the effective sample size of the worst parameter reaches minESS (200) and R-hat is below rhatTarget (1.01), and may run to four times the requested number of draws to get there. meanESS, maxDraws, settleTol, and the NUTS settings maxdepth, target_accept, maxdelta, init_scale, adapt_metric and adapt_effects are described under uncertainty = 'sample' in ctFitUncertainty, along with lower targets for a quicker approximate posterior. A setting the sampler does not use is an error. For backend='stan' the settings are passed to the control argument of stan.

control

Deprecated, use sampleControl, which takes the same settings. Still honoured, with a warning. If both give the same setting, sampleControl is used.

verbose

Integer from 0 to 2. 1 reports progress while the model fits. 2 also prints more for debugging, and keeps every progress line instead of overwriting the last one. Whether progress lines can be overwritten is detected from where the output goes. If the detection is wrong, as it can be for a Shiny app capturing the output, set options(ctsem.progress.overwrite = FALSE), or TRUE to force overwriting.

...

additional arguments to pass to stan function (backend='stan' only).

popunique

Parameters that get a variance of their own on a reduced-rank level, in addition to the poprank shared dimensions. That level's covariance is then L %*% t(L) plus a diagonal, as in factor analysis. TRUE selects every parameter varying at a level, FALSE none, and names select matrices or parameters, e.g. popunique = c(subject = 'MANIFESTMEANS'). An unnamed value applies to every level, and named entries, or a named list, apply per level. Each selected level needs a poprank below its number of varying parameters. poprank = 0 with every parameter selected gives independent random effects. Reported as popunique_<parameter>.<level>, on the same raw scale as a full-rank sd. Requires backend = 'julia' and intoverpop = 'laplace' or sampling ('none'), and must be passed by name.

popblocks

Shared dimensions in blocks, on a reduced-rank level. A list of blocks, each a list with rank, the number of shared dimensions, and effects, the parameters that load on them: TRUE for every parameter varying at the level, or names of matrices or parameters as for popunique. A parameter loads only on the dimensions of the blocks that name it, so parameters with no block in common are uncorrelated, and a parameter in no block needs its own variance (popunique). A level's rank is the sum of its blocks' ranks, so poprank need not be given, and if it is given as a number it must equal that sum. One unnamed list of blocks applies to every level, and a list named by level gives each level its own. For example, person-level item intercepts that do not covary with a latent level, but may covary with each other and with the dynamics: popblocks = list(level = list(rank = 1, effects = c('lev', 'DRIFT')), items = list(rank = 2, effects = c('MANIFESTMEANS', 'DRIFT'))). The first rank parameters of a block, in the order the model lists them, form its basis. Loadings are reported as poploading_<parameter>_dim<j>, with the dimensions numbered across the blocks in order. Requires backend = 'julia' and intoverpop = 'laplace' or sampling ('none'), and must be passed by name.

weights

Sampling weights, one per subject. Either the name of a column of datalong that is constant within subject, or a numeric vector named by subject id (or unnamed, in the order subjects first appear in the data). Each subject's likelihood, with random effects integrated out, is multiplied by its weight (a weighted pseudo-likelihood). The prior is not weighted. A weight of zero leaves the subject out. Weights are normalised to a mean of one over the weighted subjects, and standard errors come from the sandwich estimator unless optimcontrol$uncertainty says otherwise. fit$estimate$loglik is the unweighted log likelihood at the estimate, and fit$estimate$loglik_weighted the weighted one. Requires backend = 'julia' and optimisation. With nested ids, weights must be constant within each group of the outermost level. Must be passed by name.

ctstanmodel

Deprecated. Use model.

Value

A fitted object of class ctStanFit (backend='stan') or ctJuliaFit (backend='julia'), both also of class ctFit. Every fit includes $args, a list with two parts that are the same on both backends:

input

The arguments passed to ctFit(), with the defaults for those not supplied, so intoverpop may be 'auto'.

resolved

The settings the fit ran with, after defaults and 'auto' were resolved and deprecated arguments merged (such as nopriors into priors). cores is a whole number, intoverpop is 'augmented', 'laplace' or 'none', and priors is TRUE, FALSE or 'randomCorr'.

Details

For a julia fit with random effects, fit$identifiability$effects reports how much of each random effect each subject's data determine, and how many subjects' worth of information each population standard deviation rests on. An effect resting on fewer than two is named in a message, in summary() and in ctReport, with a suggestion to lower poprank or set indvarying = FALSE.

See also

ctOptimControl for the optimiser settings, ctFitUncertainty for uncertainty after a fit, ctIdentify to check which parameters the data can inform before fitting, and ctTracePlot to plot the optimisation trace of a julia fit.

Examples

# \donttest{

#generate a modern ctsem model relying heavily on defaults
model<-ctModel(type='ct',
  latentNames=c('eta1','eta2'),
  manifestNames=c('Y1','Y2'),
  MANIFESTVAR=diag(.1,2),
  TDpredNames='TD1',
  TIpredNames=c('TI1','TI2','TI3'),
  LAMBDA=diag(2))

# The default backend is julia; ctJuliaInstall() sets it up.
if (isTRUE(ctJuliaStatus()$available)) {
  fit<-ctFit(ctstantestdat, model,priors=TRUE)

  summary(fit)

  plot(fit,wait=FALSE)
}

#### extended examples

library(ctsem)
set.seed(3)

#  Data generation (run this, but no need to understand!) -----------------

Tpoints <- 20
nmanifest <- 4
nlatent <- 2
nsubjects<-20

#random effects
age <- rnorm(nsubjects) #standardised
cint1<-rnorm(nsubjects,2,.3)+age*.5
cint2 <- cint1*.5+rnorm(nsubjects,1,.2)+age*.5
tdpredeffect <- rnorm(nsubjects,5,.3)+age*.5

for(i in 1:nsubjects){
  #generating model
  gm<-ctModel(Tpoints=Tpoints,n.manifest = nmanifest,n.latent = nlatent,n.TDpred = 1,
  type='omx',
    LAMBDA = matrix(c(1,0,0,0, 0,1,.8,1.3),nrow=nmanifest,ncol=nlatent),
    DRIFT=matrix(c(-.3, .2, 0, -.5),nlatent,nlatent),
    TDPREDMEANS=matrix(c(rep(0,Tpoints-10),1,rep(0,9)),ncol=1),
    TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c(tdpredeffect[i],0),nrow=nlatent),
    DIFFUSION = matrix(c(1, 0, 0, .5),2,2),
    CINT = matrix(c(cint1[i],cint2[i]),ncol=1),
    T0VAR=diag(2,nlatent,nlatent),
    MANIFESTVAR = diag(.5, nmanifest))

  #generate data
  newdat <- ctGenerate(ctmodelobj = gm,n = 1,burnin = 2,
    dtmat=rbind(c(rep(.5,8),3,rep(.5,Tpoints-9))))
  newdat[,'id'] <- i #set id for each subject
  newdat <- cbind(newdat,age[i]) #include time independent predictor
  if(i ==1) {
    dat <- newdat[1:(Tpoints-10),] #pre intervention data
    dat2 <- newdat #including post intervention data
  }
  if(i > 1) {
    dat <- rbind(dat, newdat[1:(Tpoints-10),])
    dat2 <- rbind(dat2,newdat)
  }
}
colnames(dat)[ncol(dat)] <- 'age'
colnames(dat2)[ncol(dat)] <- 'age'


#plot generated data for sanity
plot(age)
matplot(dat[,gm$manifestNames],type='l',pch=1)
plotvar <- 'Y1'
plot(dat[dat[,'id']==1,'time'],dat[dat[,'id']==1,plotvar],type='l',
  ylim=range(dat[,plotvar],na.rm=TRUE))
for(i in 2:nsubjects){
  points(dat[dat[,'id']==i,'time'],dat[dat[,'id']==i,plotvar],type='l',col=i)
}


dat2[,gm$manifestNames][sample(1:length(dat2[,gm$manifestNames]),size = 100)] <- NA


#data structure
head(dat2)


# Model fitting -----------------------------------------------------------

##simple univariate default model

m <- ctModel(type = 'ct', manifestNames = c('Y1'), LAMBDA = diag(1))
ctModelLatex(m)

#Specify univariate linear growth curve

m1 <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  DRIFT=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror'),nrow=1,ncol=1))

ctModelLatex(m1)

#fit
if (isTRUE(ctJuliaStatus()$available)) {
  f1 <- ctFit(datalong = dat2, model = m1, optimize=TRUE, priors=FALSE)

  summary(f1)

  #plots of individual subject models v data
  ctPredict(f1,plot=TRUE,subjects=1,kalmanvec=c('y','yprior'),timestep=.01)
  ctPredict(f1,plot=TRUE,subjects=1:3,kalmanvec=c('y','ysmooth'),timestep=.01,errorvec=NA)

  #compare randomly generated data from the posterior to the observed data,
  #including the lagged covariance structure and the mean trajectory over time
  ctPostPredict(f1, wait=FALSE)
}

 ### Further example models

#Include intervention
m2 <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix(-1e-5,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror'),nrow=1,ncol=1))



#Individual differences in intervention, Bayesian estimation, covariates
m2i <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  TIpredNames = 'age',
  TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect||TRUE'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix(-1e-5,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror'),nrow=1,ncol=1))


#Including covariate effects
m2ic <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  n.TIpred = 1, TIpredNames = 'age',
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix(-1e-5,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror'),nrow=1,ncol=1))

m2ic$pars$indvarying[m2ic$pars$matrix %in% 'TDPREDEFFECT'] <- TRUE


#Include deterministic dynamics
m3 <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix('drift11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(0,nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix('t0var11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror1'),nrow=1,ncol=1))





#Add system noise to allow for fluctuations that persist in time
m3n <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix('drift11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix('diffusion',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1'),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix('t0var11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = diag(1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(0,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c(0),nrow=1,ncol=1))



#include 2nd latent process

m4 <- ctModel(n.manifest = 2,n.latent = 2, type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y1','Y2'), latentNames=c('L1','L2'),
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1',
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect1','tdpredeffect2'),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  DRIFT=matrix(c('drift11','drift21','drift12','drift22'),nrow=2,ncol=2),
  DIFFUSION=matrix(c('diffusion11','diffusion21',0,'diffusion22'),nrow=2,ncol=2),
  CINT=matrix(c('cint1','cint2'),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1','t0m2'),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix(c('t0var11','t0var21',0,'t0var22'),nrow=2,ncol=2),
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1,0,0,1),nrow=2,ncol=2),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(c(0,0),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('merror1',0,0,'merror2'),nrow=2,ncol=2))

#dynamic factor model -- fixing CINT to 0 and freeing indicator level intercepts

m3df <- ctModel(type = 'ct',
  manifestNames = c('Y2','Y3'), latentNames=c('eta1'),
  n.TDpred=1,TDpredNames = 'TD1', #this line includes the intervention
  TDPREDEFFECT=matrix(c('tdpredeffect'),nrow=1,ncol=1), #intervention effect
  DRIFT=matrix('drift11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  DIFFUSION=matrix('diffusion',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  CINT=matrix(c(0),ncol=1),
  T0MEANS=matrix(c('t0m1'),ncol=1),
  T0VAR=matrix('t0var11',nrow=1,ncol=1),
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1,'Y3loading'),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTMEANS=matrix(c('Y2_int','Y3_int'),nrow=2,ncol=1),
  MANIFESTVAR=matrix(c('Y2residual',0,0,'Y3residual'),nrow=2,ncol=2))
